newsitem.title: USA: PaineWebber sees more electric and gas M&A.
newsitem.headline: PaineWebber sees more electric and gas M&A.

text.p: PaineWebber Inc expects the pace of merger and acquisition activity in the electric utility and natural gas industry to increase as deregulation in individual states and the U.S. as a whole accelerates.

In 1991, there were just $7.0 billion worth of deals involving the electric and gas pipeline, marketing and distribution industries, but this accelerated to $40 billion in 1996 as deregulation started to come into force.
"We are going to blow through that figure and maybe see $80-$100 billion," said Ron Barone, natural gas company analyst told a news conference.

Barone and PaineWebber's electric utilities analyst Barry Abramson, both the top-ranked analysts in their sector according to Institutional Investor, expect most of the deals to come from electrics buying natural gas companies.

Abramson said there are 15 electric utilities with a market capitalisation of more than $5.0 billion, whereas there is only one gas local distribution company worth more than $3.0 billion and the rest are much lower.
"There are a lot of hungry companies with strong balance sheets and the ability to borrow money," said Abramson.
Electric companies also believe they can benefit from the natural gas business, which went through deregulation several years earlier, said Abramson.
There are also problems for electric companies acquiring other electrics due to lengthy regulatory approval processes.
"The average electric on electric merger takes 18-24 months, while gas and electric convergence happens in less than 12 months," Abramson said.

Among electric utilities that could be in the market for gas companies, Boston Edison Co is selling its power plants and has a large cash pile, as does New England Electric System, while Carolina Power & Light looks like it needs a buy because it is surrounded by large energy companies such as Duke Energy Corp, said Abramson.

New England said regulatory approvals for the $1.59 billion sale of generating assets would take six- to 12 months and the company would not have any cash immediately, although it is interested in growing is electric distribution business.
The other companies declined comment.
Potential targets among gas companies are Consolidated Natural Gas Co, Sonat Inc, Tejas Gas Corp , Southwest Gas Corp, Washington Gas Light Co and Equitable Resources Inc, Barone said.
The companies were either not available or declined comment.

Among gas companies who might be buyers, Barone says El Paso Energy is looking for an electric acquisition, Enron Corp is still on the hunt after its acquisition of Portland General Electric Co and Brooklyn Union Gas Co will have a large amount of cash after selling some assets to Long Island Power Authority.
El Paso noted it was very active in the international arena.
"El Paso owns interests in three domestic electric plants, but is always looking, the same in the pipeline assets," said a spokesman for the company.
The companies were not available to respond or declined to comment on any acquisition plans.
Others include Williams Cos Inc and UtiliCorp United Inc is also in the market, while Questar Corp is likely to do a joint venture or small acquisition.
"Questar has indicated it is actively pursuing alliances on the West Coast and Midwest and we have discussions under way, but nothing to announce at the moment," said a spokesman for Questar.
Williams said that its preferred strategy was alliances.
"We have not been on either of a deal such as the Enron and Portland (acquisition)," said a spokesman for Williams.
The other companies were either not available or declined comment.
Generally, he believes that gas companies are less likely to be major acquisitors of electrics.
"Bidding for assets in an environment that is about to become deregulated is a risky strategy. I would not know what to bid for those assets," he said.

Looking further out, PaineWebber believes the amendement in the next 18 months to two years of the Public Utilities Holding Companies Act, which places limits on acquisitions by companies such as Southern Co, will unleash a further round of merger activity.
"One of these may test the law. Even if an acquisition violates the law (at present), by the time the acquisition is approved, the law may be changed," said Abramson.
((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
